/SATURDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...
Issued at 151 AM MDT Thu Oct 29 2026

No major changes. Please see previous discussion...

Most of the area will see pleasant conditions for Halloween trick-or-
treating this year. Broad ridging will remain over the area this 
weekend, supporting above average high temperatures ranging from the 
upper 50s in Carbon and Albany counties to the low to mid 60s over 
the High Plains. Expect a mix of cloud cover and sunshine as 
plentiful moisture moves over the area aloft. A weak vort-max 
passing through the area in the southwest flow overhead will help to 
support a few afternoon and evening showers, mainly over and near 
the higher terrain, but the chance for appreciable rainfall or 
thunder is low. Due to high humidity and cloud cover, overnight low 
temperatures will be mild for this time of year, only dropping to 
the upper 30s to lower 40s east of I-25, and mid to upper 30s to the 
west. Near saturated conditions will produce the potential for some 
spooky fog to develop both Saturday morning and Saturday night. 
Sunday looks mild again, but slightly cooler than Saturday with 
skies becoming mostly cloudy ahead of the next storm system 
approaching the area. 

A complex storm system will push across the western CONUS Sunday 
into early next week. Two major players will make up this system: 
first, a strong, moisture-laden upper level low riding the 
subtropical jet stream into the southwest and second, a potent 
Pacific trough pushing into the northwest. The primary questions 
concerning the evolution of this system are if, when, and where the 
two approaching systems might merge together. Ensembles have shifted 
slightly over the last 24 hours, but have yet to converge on a 
solution. Thus, several scenarios still remain, though the 
probabilities have changed. In the first scenario (approx 40% 
chance), the two features do not merge at all. Two separate mid-
level circulations competing with one other would mean muddy forcing 
forcing for ascent and limited precipitation potential. We could 
still expect some rain and snow showers, but amounts would be modest 
(0.25" or less for Laramie, Cheyenne, Wheatland, Scottsbluff, 0.25" 
to 0.5" in Rawlins and Chadron). In the second scenario (approx 50% 
chance), the two systems merge, but this occurs a little too late 
and a little too far east for a widespread major precipitation event 
for our area. Still, it would be enough for a moderate rain event 
over western Nebraska, and some potential for accumulating snow 
especially for the elevated ridges (Cheyenne Ridge & Pine Ridge). 
The scenario in which the two systems merge early enough to produce 
a major event has decreased in probability (to around 10%) as fewer 
ensembles now show this potential. The ECMWF Extreme Forecast Index 
for QPF today has decreased slightly as well to around 0.5 to 0.6 
over much of the area. This tells us that while an anomalous event 
is still possible, only a small subset of ensemble members show 
this, keeping confidence low. 

Overall probabilities for 0.5" of liquid precipitation are the 
lowest around Laramie, Cheyenne, and Wheatland (30-40%). 
Probabilities increase both east and west, with Rawlins around a 50% 
chance to exceed 0.5" and the Sidney to Chadron corridor in the 60 
to 70% range. In addition to the uncertainty in QPF, there is also 
uncertainty in the snow levels with very marginal temperatures for 
snow over much of the area. Cooler air moving in through the event 
should lead to snow levels starting fairly high (perhaps 9000 ft) 
and then dropping overnight Sunday night and through the day Monday. 
The question is how low they can get. Thus, there is fairly good 
confidence in accumulating snow for the mountains (90+% chance for 
1" and 50% chance for 6"), but lower confidence around where most 
folks live. The best chances for 1" or more of snow outside of the 
mountains are in the valleys of Carbon and Albany counties, and the 
elevated ridges of the High Plains. 

Regardless of the precipitation outcome, a cold front will sweep 
through the area Sunday night, bringing colder and windier 
conditions into the area for Monday. Which of the above scenarios 
that ends up playing out will also affect the wind direction and 
potential for high winds. Still, there is high confidence in a windy 
day along and east of the Laramie range. About 25% of ensemble 
members have 700-mb winds sufficiently high to support widespread 
high wind potential, while the I-80 summit area has about a 50% 
chance for high winds. Look for lingering impacts in the form of 
cool temperatures and windy conditions on Tuesday, but we should 
start to lose the wind and warm up slightly by Wednesday.
